corrected_proposal.description_medium: The supplied account alleges that foreign officials and lobbyists faced pressure or incentives to buy Mar-a-Lago memberships or stay at Trump-branded properties in early 2025, followed by emoluments complaints and disclosure demands. corrected_proposal.description_long: The supplied record alleges that foreign officials and lobbyists received access at a Trump-owned property in early 2025 and that some visitors or representatives paid for stays or events there. It connects those alleged transactions with emoluments complaints and requests for disclosure. The packet’s limited reporting about visits by representatives of several countries does not itself show that any official paid for access, that a payment influenced government action, or that an ethics complaint or disclosure demand produced a finding. This draft treats the payment, access, and complaint claims as allegations supplied for internal drafting. It does not identify a verified transaction, a specific official, a payment amount, or an adjudicated conflict. Visits and publicity alone do not establish private benefit or misconduct. The entry’s date and asserted relationship among visitors, payments, and policy remain unverified and should not be stated as established fact. This is an internal draft only and publication eligibility remains false.

children.title: Trump Orders U.S. Withdrawal from the World Health Organization
children.description_short: A Jan. 20, 2025 order directs steps toward U.S. withdrawal from WHO; it does not say membership ended that day.
children.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order stating that the United States intended to withdraw from the World Health Organization. It directed officials to pause future U.S. transfers, recall and reassign personnel, identify partners for necessary WHO activities, and cease negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement while withdrawal was in progress. The order does not establish that membership ended on January 20.
children.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order stating that the United States intended to withdraw from the World Health Organization. It directed the Secretary of State and Office of Management and Budget to pause future U.S. funds, support and resources to WHO; recall and reassign government personnel or contractors working with the organization; and identify U.S. and international partners to assume necessary WHO activities. The order also directed the Secretary of State to cease negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement and amendments to the International Health Regulations while withdrawal was in progress. This is an order to pursue withdrawal, not proof that the United States left WHO on January 20. The frozen entry incorrectly said the country withdrew from both WHO and UNESCO that day; the UNESCO action is a separate later claim and is kept in a second internal draft. The order's text does not establish the broader outcome claims in the frozen synopsis, so this card does not state that U.S. departure had already removed the country from disease-surveillance networks or produced quantified public-health harms.

children.title: FBI Managers Told Up to 1,500 Staff Would Move From Headquarters
children.description_short: FBI Managers Told Up to 1,500 Staff Would Move From Headquarters
children.description_medium: On February 21, 2025, The Washington Post reported that FBI managers were told up to 1,500 staff and agents would move from headquarters to field offices. The report described a planned transfer and a stated goal of bolstering field staffing; it did not establish that the plan was completed or intended to force resignations.
children.description_long: On February 21, 2025, The Washington Post reported that FBI managers had been told that up to 1,500 staff and agents would be transferred from the bureau’s Washington headquarters to field offices around the country. The article attributed the number and message to people briefed on the announcement, who spoke anonymously because it had not been publicly announced. The report placed the move in the context of Kash Patel’s newly confirmed leadership and said he had described bolstering field-office staffing as a priority. This supports a planned transfer and the stated rationale of shifting personnel toward field operations. It does not show that all 1,500 transfers occurred, that the FBI relocated its headquarters out of Washington, or that the plan was designed to force employees to resign. Those stronger claims appeared in the original combined entry without support in the cited report. This child keeps the transfer plan dated separately from pre-confirmation DOJ actions and later polygraph-based leak investigations. Its effects on individual employees and field-office staffing are unknown.

children.description_short: Trump-Era Agencies Expand Polygraph Use in Leak Investigations, Report Says
children.description_medium: The Washington Post reported on April 28, 2025 that national security agencies in the Trump administration were expanding investigations into alleged media leaks, with polygraph tests used in some cases. The report attributed fears of intimidation to current and former officials. Its available account does not establish FBI-wide testing or that Patel personally ordered each examination.
children.description_long: The Washington Post reported on April 28, 2025 that national security agencies across the Trump administration were expanding investigations into alleged media leaks and that some investigations used polygraph examinations. The report said current and former officials described the crackdown as creating a climate of fear and intimidation. The article’s title names the FBI, while its opening text describes a wider group of agencies; this entry therefore uses that broader scope and does not state that every FBI employee was tested or that Patel personally ordered each examination. The report records an investigative practice, not a finding that a particular employee leaked information or that a polygraph result proved misconduct. It also does not establish the number of examinations, the number of agencies involved, or any final disciplinary outcomes. This issue belongs in a separate record from January personnel directives made before Patel became FBI director and from the February headquarters-transfer plan. The available excerpt supports the reported expansion and use of tests in some cases; details beyond that remain unverified.

children.title: DOJ Files Judicial-Misconduct Complaint Against Judge James Boasberg
children.description_short: The Justice Department filed a misconduct complaint against Judge Boasberg on July 29, 2025; the Sixth Circuit dismissed it in December.
children.description_medium: On July 29, 2025, the Justice Department filed a judicial-misconduct complaint against Chief Judge James Boasberg with the D.C. Circuit’s Judicial Council. The complaint alleged misconduct based on remarks at a March Judicial Conference and Boasberg’s handling of litigation over removals under the Alien Enemies Act. A Sixth Circuit order later dismissed it, citing insufficient evidence and other Rule 11 grounds; the allegations were not findings against Boasberg.
children.description_long: On July 29, 2025, the Justice Department filed a judicial-misconduct complaint against Chief Judge James Boasberg with the D.C. Circuit’s Judicial Council. The complaint alleged that comments Boasberg reportedly made during a March Judicial Conference and his rulings in litigation over removals under the Alien Enemies Act violated judicial ethics canons. Those statements were allegations in the complaint, not findings. After the proceeding was transferred to the Sixth Circuit, Chief Judge Jeffrey Sutton dismissed it on December 19, 2025. The order said the complaint lacked sufficient evidence and was related in part to the merits of rulings; it also noted that DOJ had not supplied an attachment it cited as evidence. The order resolved the misconduct complaint, not the separate underlying deportation litigation. Reuters reported the filing on July 28, while the Sixth Circuit order gives July 29 as the filing date; this card uses the court’s date. The complaint’s dismissal is stated without implying that Boasberg committed misconduct or that the underlying litigation ended on that date.

children.title: Trump Administration Makes 34 Emergency Requests to the Supreme Court by March 2026
children.description_short: A Brennan Center tally says the administration sought emergency Supreme Court intervention 34 times by March 2026; 25 requests had decisions, with an 80% win rate.
children.description_medium: A Brennan Center tally published April 28, 2026, reported that by March the second Trump administration had asked the Supreme Court to intervene 34 times when lower courts blocked parts of its agenda. The Court had issued 25 shadow-docket decisions on those requests and ruled for the administration in 80 percent of them. These are the Center’s counts; they do not establish that each request produced a final merits judgment or a lasting policy change.
children.description_long: By March 2026, the second Trump administration had asked the Supreme Court to intervene 34 times after lower courts blocked parts of its agenda, according to a Brennan Center for Justice tally published April 28, 2026. The Center reported that the Court issued 25 shadow-docket decisions on those requests and ruled for the administration in 80 percent of them. This is a count of emergency requests and resulting decisions, not a count of final merits judgments or proof that every requested policy became permanent. The reported win rate has 25 decisions as its denominator; the source does not claim that all 34 requests received decisions by that date. Because this record combines separate matters from the Boasberg complaint, it treats the tally as a distinct administration-wide pattern over time. The applications’ use of an established emergency process does not alone show misconduct, and the count does not supply individual case outcomes or quantified harms. It is attributed to the Brennan Center, whose policy article advances reforms to Supreme Court practice. The card therefore records its measure and scope without presenting the Center’s characterization of the docket as a court finding.
